timelineEvents.title: Arrival in New York en route to Los Angeles
timelineEvents.label: 24 Oct 1934 · Arrival in New York
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper arrives in New York from France with Eleonora, holding a temporary visa and travelling onward to Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper and his wife Eleonora sailed from Le Havre on 17 October 1934 aboard the S.S. Champlain in second cabin class and reached New York on 24 October. Their non-immigrant visas had been issued in Paris on 15 October, numbered in a single series with the Jurmanns’ (NI 1581–1584), and the manifest records Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer as having paid the passage and as the party they were joining in Culver City. Kaper gave his occupation as musician and declared that he meant to stay about eight months and then return, without seeking United States citizenship. David Blum of the Culver Export Corporation met them in New York, and they left for Hollywood on 27 October.

timelineEvents.title: Legal Permanent Entry
timelineEvents.label: 1 Nov 1935 · Permanent U.S. entry
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper enters the United States for permanent residence through Calexico with Eleonora.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Enters for permanent residence at Calexico, California, from Mexicali on 1 November 1935, travelling on foot with Eleonora. The manifest records 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood, as his U.S. destination; his Declaration of Intention four months later records the same address as his residence. The crossing followed the Immigration and Naturalization Service pre-examination procedure: Kaper gave the Commercial Hotel in Mexicali as his last permanent residence abroad and entered on a consular immigration visa, C.I.V. no. 1/24, issued there under Section 5 of the Immigration Act of 1924 and charged to the Polish quota. The manifest records his previous stay in California from 24 October 1934 to 20 October 1935, and his Polish passport no. 10568, issued by the Consulate General in Paris on 5 August 1934 and expired on 25 August 1935.

timelineEvents.title: Hollywood debut
timelineEvents.label: 1935 · Hollywood debut
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper makes his Hollywood debut at MGM, contributing to Escapade and other major studio projects.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The first American score documented here is “Escapade” (dir. Robert Z. Leonard) with William Powell and Luise Rainer. Press hails “Two New Composers” of Kiepura’s European hits. Songs also for Marx Brothers’ “A Night at the Opera” (with Ned Washington) and “Mutiny on the Bounty”. MGM engaged Kaper at first as a song specialist rather than as a film composer, and by his own account he moved only gradually from songwriter to composer of scores. For Escapade, which opened in July 1935, he supplied a single number, “You’re All I Need”, to words by Gus Kahn.

timelineEvents.title: San Francisco success and Three Smart Girls
timelineEvents.label: 1936 · San Francisco and Three Smart Girls
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The title song from San Francisco becomes a major hit, while Kaper and Jurmann also contribute to Universal’s Three Smart Girls.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The success of San Francisco made Kaper and Jurmann more visible in Hollywood and helped establish Kaper’s reputation beyond the MGM studio system. The event also includes Three Smart Girls, the Universal production associated with Deanna Durbin and Joseph Pasternak. Tommy Dorsey’s recording of the title song stood third in the Victor column of The Billboard’s ten best records for the week ended 3 August 1936.

timelineEvents.title: Declarations of Intention
timelineEvents.label: 4 Feb 1936 · Declarations of Intention
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Bronisław and Eleonora Kaper file Declarations of Intention to become U.S. citizens in Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: On 4 February 1936, Bronisław Kaper and Eleonora Kaper each filed a Declaration of Intention in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, Los Angeles. Bronisław Kaper’s declaration records him as residing at Château des Fleurs, 6626 Franklin Ave., Hollywood. A Certificate of Arrival issued on 2 January 1936 had confirmed the Calexico entry, in a document valid, as its own form states, for naturalisation purposes only; its number, 23-46078, recurs on the declaration and ties the two documents together.

timelineEvents.title: European Film Fund
timelineEvents.label: 1938 · European Film Fund
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper participates in the European Film Fund, helping support refugees from the European film community.
timelineEvents.longDescription: The European Film Fund was established in 1938 by Paul Kohner, Ernst Lubitsch, and Carl Laemmle to aid refugees arriving from Europe. Kaper participated in the Fund despite his relatively secure position at MGM. A surviving donor list for 1 May 1941–30 April 1942 records “Kaper, Bronislaw” and a contribution of $120, providing direct documentary evidence of his involvement.

timelineEvents.title: End of an era
timelineEvents.label: 1938 · Jurmann–Kaper era ends
timelineEvents.shortDescription: The Jurmann–Kaper collaboration ends amicably as Hollywood’s musical priorities change.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Amicable end of Jurmann–Kaper collaboration; industry changes reduce demand for thematic songs.

timelineEvents.title: New chapter
timelineEvents.label: 1939 · Solo MGM chapter begins
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper remains at MGM and begins a new solo chapter as a film composer.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper stayed at MGM after the partnership with Jurmann ended and moved, by his own account gradually, from writing songs to composing film scores.

timelineEvents.title: MGM markets Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”
timelineEvents.label: MGM’s “Viennese” label
timelineEvents.shortDescription: American studio publicity recast Kaper and Jurmann as a Viennese composing team, turning “Vienna” into a promotional brand rather than a biographical fact.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Soon after their arrival at MGM, the American press and studio publicity presented Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”. The label suited MGM’s first use of the duo in Escapade, a Hollywood remake of the Viennese film Maskerade, but it was biographically misleading for Kaper, whose career had developed in Warsaw and Berlin. The event marks the moment when Hollywood began to translate his European professional history into a marketable studio identity. The label outlasted their arrival: in December 1936 the Viennese paper Telegraf itself wrote of “die Wiener Komponisten Kaper und Jurmann”.
